title: Justice Samuel Alito Recuses Himself from High-Stakes Climate Case Involving Energy Giants
snippet: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will step aside from an upcoming legal battle against Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy over climate change liabilities.
content:
WASHINGTON — Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will not participate in a pivotal upcoming legal battle over whether oil companies can be held liable under state laws for climate change damages, court officials announced Monday.

The dispute, scheduled for oral arguments on Oct. 5—the opening day of the Supreme Court's new term—involves a bid by Exxon Mobil Corp. and Suncor Energy to block a lawsuit brought by local officials in Boulder, Colorado. The landmark case is expected to establish a crucial legal precedent affecting dozens of similar climate harm lawsuits filed by state and municipal governments across the country.

Conflict Questions and Financial Disclosures

In a letter dispatched to attorneys representing both the energy firms and the Colorado officials, Supreme Court Clerk Scott Harris confirmed Alito's withdrawal without providing an explicit rationale.

"I am writing to inform the parties that Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case," Harris wrote.

Although Alito does not directly hold shares in Exxon or Suncor, his most recent financial disclosure forms show stock ownership in other energy titans, including ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. Both of those companies are currently defending themselves in separate, parallel climate suits. Ethics watchdogs and environmental groups had previously called on the conservative justice to step aside due to potential conflicts of interest.

A Broader Precedent for Fossil Fuel Suits

The lawsuit originated in 2018 when Boulder officials filed suit against Exxon and Suncor, alleging the energy companies contributed significantly to global warming harms affecting local infrastructure and ecosystems. The core legal question before the nation's highest court centers on whether federal law preempts local and state-level claims seeking monetary damages for greenhouse gas emissions.

Justices have also instructed attorneys to address whether the high court has proper jurisdiction to rule on the dispute at this preliminary stage. The Trump administration previously filed briefs backing the energy companies, maintaining that federal law precludes local municipal claims of this nature.
